title: Data & Methods
text: The Reporting Carrier On-Time Performance table from the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics (TranStats) has one row per domestic flight operated by large US airlines. It records scheduled and actual times, delays, cancellations, diversions and their causes. My assigned month was January 2024: one CSV of 247 MB, 547,271 rows and 110 columns.

title: Data & Methods
text: The Reporting Carrier On-Time Performance table from the US Bureau of Transportation Statistics (TranStats) has one row per domestic flight operated by large US airlines. It records scheduled and actual times, delays, cancellations, diversions and their causes. My assigned month was January 2024: one CSV of 247 MB, 547,271 rows and 110 columns.

title: Data & Methods
text:
Loading pipeline on AWS
The fact table is too large for MySQL Workbench’s import wizard, so it was loaded from a cloud machine with MySQL’s bulk loader:






flowchart LR
    A["BTS TranStats<br>zip download"] --> B["Laptop<br>al_perf.csv"]
    B -->|scp| C["AWS EC2<br>Amazon Linux"]
    C -->|mysqlimport| D[("AWS RDS<br>MySQL 8, schema FAA")]
    E["Canvas<br>6 dimension CSVs"] -->|Workbench import wizard| D
    D -->|SQL queries| F["Result CSVs"]
    F --> G["Quarto website<br>Python + Plotly"]







Created schema FAA (UTF-8) and the fact table al_perf with the course’s CreateFactTable.sql.
Copied al_perf.csv to an EC2 instance with scp, installed the MySQL/MariaDB client, and ran the bulk load against the RDS endpoint. It loaded 547,271 records, the CSV’s row count minus its header:
mysqlimport --local --compress --user=admin -p --host=<rds-endpoint> \
  --fields-terminated-by=',' --fields-optionally-enclosed-by='"' \
  --ignore-lines=1 FAA al_perf.csv
Loaded the six dimension tables with Workbench’s Table Data Import Wizard.
Terminated the EC2 instance (and kept the RDS database) to avoid charges.
Ran the 7 queries, exported each result to CSV, and built this site from those CSVs with Quarto, pandas and Plotly. The site never connects to the database.

title: Data & Methods
text:
Data-cleaning decisions
Blank numbers become zeros. In the CSV, a cancelled flight that never left the gate has empty DepTime and DepDelay fields. mysqlimport stores an empty numeric field as 0 and raises a warning (that’s most of the ~250,000 import warnings). The database therefore says those 19,784 flights departed “0 minutes late”. For every departure-delay calculation I keep only rows with a recorded departure time, DepTime <> ''. Without that filter, airports and airlines hit hardest by cancellations would look more punctual than they were. (605 cancelled flights did leave the gate before being cancelled. They keep their real recorded delay.)
Early departures. Problem 4 says to count early departures as 0 minutes. I use GREATEST(DepDelay, 0), which equals BTS’s own DepDelayMinutes column, and apply the same rule in Problem 5 and in the site’s average-delay charts so all averages are comparable.
The header row. The course instructions run mysqlimport without --ignore-lines=1, which loads the CSV header as one junk row (Year = 0, FlightDate = the text ‘FlightDate’). I skipped it at load time. If it had been loaded, DELETE FROM al_perf WHERE Year = 0; would remove it.
What counts as a flight. BTS sets Flights = 1 on every row, including cancelled ones, so flight counts (Problems 3 and 7) use COUNT(*) over all scheduled flights.
Ties. Problems 5 and 6b use RANK(), which keeps ties rather than picking one row arbitrarily. Problem 5 had no ties. In Problem 6b, 5 airports had two reasons tied for first, giving 301 rows for 296 airports.

title: Data & Methods
text:
Verification
Every answer was recomputed independently with pandas directly from the raw CSV (not through MySQL), and the results matched exactly.

title: Data & Methods
text:
Limitations

One month. January has winter weather and, in 2024, an unusual safety grounding. These patterns should not be read as typical for the whole year.
Small samples. Averages for small airports and rare airline–airport pairs rest on very few flights. The site reports those counts alongside the averages.
Cause vs. coincidence. The link between carrier cancellations and the 737 MAX 9 grounding comes from timing, airline and airport patterns. The dataset has no aircraft-type column, so it can’t prove which aircraft was cancelled.

Tools

title: The 7 SQL Questions
text: All queries run against schema FAA: the fact table al_perf (547,271 flights, January 2024) plus the dimension tables L_AIRLINE_ID, L_AIRPORT, L_WEEKDAYS and L_CANCELATION. The full submission file is hw4_cheng_zhiyang_zc385.sql.

title: The 7 SQL Questions
text:
Problem 1
Find maximal departure delay in minutes for each airline. Sort results from smallest to largest maximum delay. Output airline names and values of the delay.


SELECT a.Name AS airline_name,
       MAX(p.DepDelay) AS max_departure_delay_minutes
FROM al_perf p
JOIN L_AIRLINE_ID a ON a.ID = p.DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline
WHERE p.DepTime <> ''
GROUP BY a.ID, a.Name
ORDER BY max_departure_delay_minutes ASC;

Problem 2
Find maximal early departures in minutes for each airline. Sort results from largest to smallest. Output airline names.
An early departure has a negative DepDelay, so the earliest departure is -MIN(DepDelay).


SELECT a.Name AS airline_name,
       -MIN(p.DepDelay) AS max_early_departure_minutes
FROM al_perf p
JOIN L_AIRLINE_ID a ON a.ID = p.DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline
WHERE p.DepTime <> ''
  AND p.DepDelay < 0
GROUP BY a.ID, a.Name
ORDER BY max_early_departure_minutes DESC;

title: The 7 SQL Questions
text:
Problem 3
Rank days of the week by the number of flights performed by all airlines on that day (1 is the busiest). Output the day of the week names, number of flights and ranks in the rank increasing order.
Each row of al_perf is one flight (BTS sets Flights = 1 on every row, cancelled ones included), so the count is COUNT(*). RANK() assigns the ranks.


SELECT w.Day AS day_of_week,
       COUNT(*) AS num_flights,
       RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS day_rank
FROM al_perf p
JOIN L_WEEKDAYS w ON w.Code = p.DayOfWeek
GROUP BY w.Code, w.Day
ORDER BY day_rank;

title: The 7 SQL Questions
text:
Problem 4
Find the airport that has the highest average departure delay among all airports. Consider 0 minutes delay for flights that departed early. Output one line of results: the airport name, code, and average delay.
GREATEST(DepDelay, 0) turns early departures into 0 minutes. Airports are origin (departure) airports.


SELECT ap.Name AS airport_name,
       p.Origin AS airport_code,
       ROUND(AVG(GREATEST(p.DepDelay, 0)), 2) AS avg_departure_delay_minutes
FROM al_perf p
JOIN L_AIRPORT ap ON ap.Code = p.Origin
WHERE p.DepTime <> ''
GROUP BY p.Origin, ap.Name
ORDER BY AVG(GREATEST(p.DepDelay, 0)) DESC
LIMIT 1;

North Central West Virginia airport (CKB), Clarksburg/Fairmont, WV: 86.00 minutes. That average comes from only 15 departures. Among airports with at least 1,000 departures the highest was Des Moines (35.3 minutes). The story plots every airport.

title: The 7 SQL Questions
text:
Problem 5
For each airline find an airport where it has the highest average departure delay. Output an airline name, a name of the airport that has the highest average delay, and the value of that average delay.
A CTE computes each airline’s average delay at each airport (early = 0, as in Problem 4). RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY airline ...) then keeps the top airport per airline. There were no ties, so it returns one row per airline.


WITH airline_airport AS (
    SELECT p.DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline AS airline_id,
           p.Origin AS airport_code,
           AVG(GREATEST(p.DepDelay, 0)) AS avg_delay
    FROM al_perf p
    WHERE p.DepTime <> ''
    GROUP BY p.DOT_ID_Reporting_Airline, p.Origin
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT airline_id, airport_code, avg_delay,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY airline_id ORDER BY avg_delay DESC) AS rnk
    FROM airline_airport
)
SELECT a.Name AS airline_name,
       ap.Name AS airport_name,
       ROUND(r.avg_delay, 2) AS avg_departure_delay_minutes
FROM ranked r
JOIN L_AIRLINE_ID a ON a.ID = r.airline_id
JOIN L_AIRPORT ap ON ap.Code = r.airport_code
WHERE r.rnk = 1
ORDER BY r.avg_delay DESC;

title: The 7 SQL Questions
text:
Problem 6b
If it does, what was the most frequent reason for each departure airport? Output airport name, the most frequent reason, and the number of cancelations for that reason.
The query counts cancellations by (airport, reason), ranks the reasons within each airport and keeps rank 1. 296 airports had at least one cancellation. At 5 of them two reasons tie for first place, and both are listed, so the result has 301 rows. The first 20 are shown below; the CSV has all of them.


WITH airport_reason AS (
    SELECT p.Origin AS airport_code,
           p.CancellationCode,
           COUNT(*) AS num_cancellations
    FROM al_perf p
    WHERE p.Cancelled = 1
    GROUP BY p.Origin, p.CancellationCode
),
ranked AS (
    SELECT airport_code, CancellationCode, num_cancellations,
           RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY airport_code ORDER BY num_cancellations DESC) AS rnk
    FROM airport_reason
)
SELECT ap.Name AS airport_name,
       c.Reason AS most_frequent_reason,
       r.num_cancellations
FROM ranked r
JOIN L_AIRPORT ap ON ap.Code = r.airport_code
JOIN L_CANCELATION c ON c.Code = r.CancellationCode
WHERE r.rnk = 1
ORDER BY r.num_cancellations DESC, airport_name, most_frequent_reason;

title: The 7 SQL Questions
text:
Problem 7
Build a report that for each day output average number of flights considering the current and the previous two days.
A 3-day moving average uses the window ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW over daily flight counts. January 1 and 2 have no earlier days in this dataset, so their averages use the 1 or 2 days that exist.


WITH daily AS (
    SELECT FlightDate, COUNT(*) AS num_flights
    FROM al_perf
    GROUP BY FlightDate
)
SELECT FlightDate AS flight_date,
       num_flights,
       ROUND(AVG(num_flights) OVER (ORDER BY FlightDate
                                    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS avg_flights_3day
FROM daily
ORDER BY FlightDate;

title: One Month, Two Shocks
text: January 2024 looks like an ordinary winter month at first. But when I loaded every domestic flight into a MySQL database on AWS and asked it questions, two separate disruptions stood out: a wave of winter storms, and the grounding of one aircraft type that hit two airlines especially hard. This page tells that story. The 7 SQL questions page gives the exact queries and answers.

title: One Month, Two Shocks
section: 1. Two shocks hit the same month
text:
1. Two shocks hit the same month
Every cancelled flight in the data carries a reason code. Weather means the airline cancelled because of the weather. Carrier means the cause was within the airline’s control (crew, maintenance, aircraft). National Air System means air traffic control or airport operations. Plotting them by day shows two very different patterns.


                            
                                            



Weather (orange) came in bursts. Storms on January 9 and again from January 12 to 16 drove cancellations to 2,962 on January 15 (Martin Luther King Jr. Day). The five days from Jan 12 to Jan 16 alone hold 46% of the whole month’s cancellations. The average departure delay that day was 51 minutes, compared with about 9 minutes on a calm day like January 5.
Carrier cancellations (blue) behaved like a plateau, not a storm. They averaged 16 per day from January 1 to 5. Overnight they jumped to about 335 per day and stayed there until January 27, and then they dropped. Weather doesn’t behave like that. A policy decision does.

title: One Month, Two Shocks
text:
2. One aircraft type, two airlines
On the evening of January 5, a door plug blew out of an Alaska Airlines Boeing 737 MAX 9 shortly after takeoff from Portland (Flight 1282). The next day the FAA grounded 171 MAX 9 jets with the same door plug design. Alaska (65 jets) and United (79 jets) flew most of them in the US. Alaska resumed MAX 9 flights on January 26 and United on January 27.


                            
                                            



Of the 7,736 cancellations blamed on the airline itself, 6,895 (89%) were Alaska or United. During the grounding (January 6–27) those two airlines averaged about 300 carrier-caused cancellations a day. The other 13 airlines combined averaged 33 a day, up from 13 a day before it. Alaska cancelled 17.6% of all its January flights, roughly 1 in 6. Delta, for comparison, cancelled 0.6%.

The outside events line up with the database. The plateau starts on January 6, the day the grounding order was issued. United’s line falls on January 28, the day after its MAX 9s returned. The data alone can’t prove that a given flight was cancelled because of the grounding. But no other explanation fits two airlines, one date range and one cancellation code this well.

title: One Month, Two Shocks
section: 3. Delays and cancellations are different ways to fail
text:
3. Delays and cancellations are different ways to fail
One of the assignment questions asks for each airline’s longest delay. That turns out to be a poor measure of service. American had the single worst delay of the month: one flight left 3,125 minutes (52 hours) late. Alaska’s worst delay was only 684 minutes, the second-shortest of any airline. Yet Alaska cancelled more flights than anyone. Putting the typical delay and the cancellation rate side by side shows the real trade-offs:


                            
                                            



Alaska and United sit high on the chart. Their problem was cancelled flights, and only moderate delays.
American, Frontier and JetBlue sit far right. They cancelled few flights (1.6–2.2%) but were often late: American’s average departure delay was 25.5 minutes, the worst of any airline.
Delta sits in the best corner: the lowest cancellation rate (0.64%) and a below-average delay (14.8 minutes). Southwest, by far the largest airline (115,389 flights), kept its average delay to 14.0 minutes.

A single worst-case number (Problem 1) or a single average can’t show this. You need both measures, and you need to know how many flights sit behind each.

title: One Month, Two Shocks
section: 4. Watch the sample size: small airports produce extreme averages
text:
4. Watch the sample size: small airports produce extreme averages
Problem 4 asks which airport had the highest average departure delay. The answer is North Central West Virginia (CKB) in Clarksburg/Fairmont, at 86 minutes. But CKB had only 15 departures in the whole month, so a few badly delayed flights decide its average. The scatter shows that pattern for every airport:


                            
                                            


Small airports, on the left, spread from 0 to 86 minutes. Big airports, on the right, cluster between about 10 and 35 minutes. Among the 86 airports with at least 1,000 departures, the worst was Des Moines (DSM), 35.3 minutes. Iowa had heavy snow and extreme cold in mid-January. The best were in California: San Jose (9.6), Long Beach (9.6) and Oakland (10.5). The same caution applies to Problem 5: Spirit’s “worst airport” is based on a single flight. See Problem 5.

title: One Month, Two Shocks
section: 5. The reason behind cancellations depends on whose hub it is
text:
5. The reason behind cancellations depends on whose hub it is


                            
                                            


At most airports, weather was the most common reason for cancelling. That was true at 253 of the 296 airports that had any cancellations (counting ties), including Chicago O’Hare, Dallas/Fort Worth, Washington National and LaGuardia. But at Seattle (90% carrier-caused), San Francisco, Newark, Los Angeles and Houston, the airline was the main cause. These are Alaska’s and United’s hubs. The aircraft grounding shows up in the airport data too.

title: One Month, Two Shocks
section: 6. If you can choose when to fly
text:
6. If you can choose when to fly


                            
                                            


Delays build up during the day. Each late flight makes that aircraft’s next flight late too. Of flights scheduled to leave between 6 and 7 a.m., 9.9% left 15+ minutes late. For flights scheduled between 7 and 8 p.m. it was 32.1%, more than three times as many.


                            
                                            


Problem 3 ranks Monday as the busiest day, but that’s mostly a calendar effect. January 2024 started on a Monday, so it had five Mondays, Tuesdays and Wednesdays (blue) and only four of every other day. Per day, Friday (18,526 flights) and Thursday (18,478) were busiest, and Saturday was clearly the quietest day (15,879). The Saturday dips show up as a weekly rhythm in the 3-day moving average (Problem 7).

title: One Month, Two Shocks
text:
What to take away

Look at causes, not just totals. The month’s 20,389 cancellations came from two different events. Splitting them by reason code and date separated a weather story from an aircraft-safety story.
Most airline-caused cancellations trace to one grounding. Alaska and United account for 89% of them, and the pattern starts and ends on the dates the MAX 9s left and returned to service.
A worst case or an average needs its denominator. The worst-delay airport and several “worst airport per airline” answers rest on a handful of flights. Reporting the counts alongside averages keeps a dashboard honest.
Fly early in the day if you can. Morning departures were about three times less likely to leave 15+ minutes late than evening ones.


How the numbers were produced: the January 2024 file from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics was copied to an AWS EC2 instance, loaded into MySQL on Amazon RDS with mysqlimport, joined with 6 lookup (dimension) tables, and analyzed with SQL (window functions and CTEs). Details and data-cleaning decisions are on the Data & methods page.
